text: This is ReadyHome. It asks a family a few questions, tells them how ready they are for an emergency, and gives them three small steps to get readier.

I grew up in a multi-generational household. In an emergency, a toddler, a grandparent with a walker, and a dog each need something completely different. The official guidance for each of them lives in a different P D F, and nothing tells one family where they actually stand.
Sunny runs the survey. One short question at a time, with tappable answers, or your own words.

Before the real answers, let me try to break it. A prompt injection is caught before it ever reaches the model, so the attack costs nothing. No prompt leaks, and the survey picks up where it left off.

Here is the part I care about most. When the questions get personal, about mobility, medical equipment, or needing help to evacuate, Sunny pushes the sunglasses up and drops the emoji. The app decides that in plain code, not by asking the model to be tactful.
The state question is a searchable list, so nobody has to guess a format.
The rest of the questions cover what the household already has. Water, medication, backup power, and a way to get out.
There is the score, out of ten. It only counts what applies to this household, so a family with no pets loses no points for pet supplies. The breakdown underneath shows exactly where the gaps are.

Three steps at a time, biggest win first. Each one says what it is worth, what it costs, and links to the official source it came from. The app cannot invent a step or a link. Both come from a fixed knowledge base, and a verifier drops anything that is not in it.
And when you actually do one, you tick off what you did, and the next best step moves up to take its place.

Every session reports what it cost to run. This one is about fourteen cents: the token counts are measured, the dollar rate is an assumption. The scoring and the ranking are plain Python, so they cost nothing at all. ReadyHome. One small step at a time.
